title: The alphabet: twenty-two consonants

objectives.can: Name each of the twenty-two consonants, give its sound, and read from right to left.

explanation.summary: Biblical Hebrew is written in an alphabet of twenty-two letters, from right to left. Every word you will read in this course is made of them, so the first job is to know each letter by sight, by name and by sound.

sections.heading: Twenty-two letters, all of them consonants
body: The first table of this lesson lists the twenty-two letters in their traditional order, with the name each letter has in English, the usual way of writing it in Latin letters (its transliteration), and its sound in two pronunciation traditions. The order is the order of the Hebrew alphabet, the same order that the alphabetical poems of the Bible follow.

Every one of the twenty-two letters is a consonant. The original text was written with consonants only, so a reader had to know the language to supply the vowels. Later scribes added small marks around the letters to show the vowels; those marks are the subject of lessons H0.2.1 and H0.2.2. For now, read past them and look at the letters.

Learn the letters themselves, not their transliterations. A Hebrew text never prints transliteration, so the aim is to look at a word and see its letters at once, not to turn it into English letters first. The transliteration column is an aid that scholars use when they write about Hebrew in Latin letters. It is a convention, and different books use different symbols for the same letter, so you may hide the column in the app.

head: Direction
What it means
rows: A line begins at the right-hand edge of the page and runs left. The first letter of a word is its rightmost letter.
A Hebrew book opens from the right: its first page is where an English book has its last.
A word is read letter by letter from its right-hand end to its left-hand end, and the next word lies to its left.

sections.heading: Reading from right to left
body: Look at the first word of the Bible. Its first letter is the rightmost one, a bet, and its last is the leftmost, a tav. When you check a word letter by letter, start at the right and move left.
Hebrew has no capital letters and no italics. A name looks like any other word.

sections.heading: Two ways of pronouncing the letters
body: The sounds in the table are given in two columns. 'Modern' is the pronunciation of Israeli Hebrew, which is the one most learners meet first. 'Tiberian' is the pronunciation that scholars reconstruct from the work of the Masoretes of Tiberias, who preserved the text and its vowels. It is a reconstruction, so its details are disputed, and some of the descriptions in the table are the usual scholarly view rather than a certainty.

The two traditions agree on most letters. They differ on a few: ו, ח, ט, ע, צ, ק, ת, and on the letters ב ג ד כ פ ת, each of which can have a harder or a softer sound. Lesson H0.2.3 says when. In this lesson you need only know that the difference exists and that the spelling of a word never changes with the pronunciation.

sections.heading: Letters that you cannot hear
body: Two letters, א and ע, are consonants that Modern Hebrew speakers mostly do not pronounce at all, or pronounce as a slight stop. They are still letters, and a word is spelled with them. In the Tiberian tradition ע is a real throat consonant. The letter ה is pronounced h at the start of a word and is often silent at the end of one.

misunderstandings: The vowels are not letters in this alphabet. A word such as בָּרָא shows only three letters, ב, ר and א; the small marks around them are the vowel points.
The name of a letter is not the sound it makes. Bet is a name; the sound of ב is b (or v).

Transliteration is a help for talking about a word, not a spelling to learn. Hebrew words are always learned in Hebrew letters, and the same Hebrew letter may be written in several ways in Latin letters.
The sounds in the table are a teaching convention, not a recording of how ancient speakers talked. The Tiberian column is a scholarly reconstruction and is itself uncertain in places.

deeper.heading: Where the letters came from
body: The Hebrew alphabet descends from the alphabet used in Phoenicia, which the Greeks also borrowed. The names alef and bet are from the same source as the Greek alpha and beta. The script printed in Hebrew Bibles today is the square script, which Jews adopted in the last centuries before the common era; earlier Hebrew inscriptions use a different, older script.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: IN THE beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Read the first highlighted word from the right. Its letters are bet, resh, alef, shin, yod, tav: six consonants, whatever marks sit around them. The next word is made of the first three of these letters again: bet, resh, alef. The small marks under and beside them are vowel points, and they are what make the two words differ in sound.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: IN THE beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The first highlighted word is alef followed by tav, read from the right. The second has the same two letters with a vav in front of them; that vav is a small word meaning 'and', written as part of the next word. Notice that the vav stands at the right-hand edge, because the first thing you read is on the right.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And God saw the light, that it was good; and God divided the light from the darkness.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: טוֹב begins with tet, a letter that Modern Hebrew pronounces like tav. Then comes vav (here with a dot above it, which is a vowel mark, not a letter) and bet. The word beside it, כִּי, is kaf and yod. Compare the shapes of kaf and bet: they are easy to confuse, and lesson H0.1.2 sets them side by side.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And God called the light Day, and the darkness He called Night. And there was evening and there was morning, one day.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Three words of one short verse. עֶרֶב is ayin, resh, bet; the first letter is silent in Modern Hebrew speech but is a letter of the word. בֹקֶר is bet, qof, resh. אֶחָד is alef, het, dalet: its middle letter is het, the throat sound, and its last is dalet.

check.explain: הוּא is ה he, ו vav and א alef. The first letter is he, with a gap between its leg and its roof; het (ח) is a different letter with a closed top.

reading.why: Three short verses of plain words (light, good, day, night, evening, morning), with letters you now know: alef, bet, het, tet, qof, resh. Do not try to translate; read the letters one by one from the right, and look at the English beside the verse afterwards.
